subject: math
title: Grade 5 Probability Experiments
seo_title: Grade 5 Probability Experiments Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Probability experiments, single events or outcomes
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 math worksheets on probability experiments for the BC curriculum: outcomes and events, impossible to certain, probability as a fraction, spinners and bags, predicting and comparing with results, and fair games. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Probability = the outcomes you want ÷ all the outcomes. It goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
key_sub: List the outcomes carefully, and on a spinner look at the size of each part, not the number of colours. A game is fair when every player has the same chance.
body_html:
Outcomes

An outcome is one result that can happen. Rolling a number cube has 6 outcomes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Each roll is one trial. An event is a group of outcomes, like “roll an even number” (2, 4, 6).

Example 1

Which outcomes make the event “roll a number less than 3”?

Less than 3 means smaller than 3. The 3 itself does not count.

Answer: 1 and 2

Likelihood words

We describe how likely an event is with five words: impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely and certain. As numbers, they go from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

Probability as a fraction

When the outcomes are equally likely:

probability = number of outcomes you want ÷ total number of outcomes

Example 2

What is the probability of taking a red marble from this bag?

There are 3 red marbles and 8 marbles altogether. Compare with all 8, not with the 5 blue.

Answer: 38, which is less than 12, so red is unlikely

Spinners: look at the size of the parts

Example 3

What is the probability of landing on red?

Red covers half of the spinner. Do not count colours: 3 colours does not mean 13 each.

Answer: 12

Predict, then compare

Use the probability to predict: a 6 has a probability of 16, so in 60 rolls expect about 60 ÷ 6 = 10 sixes. Then do the experiment and compare. Results are usually close to the prediction, but rarely exactly the same. More trials usually get closer.

Coin tossesHeadsFraction of heads
107710
209920
200104104200

Fair games

A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning. Win on even, lose on odd with a number cube: 36 and 36, so it is fair.

Example 4

Liam wins on 1 or 2. Emma wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6. Is the game fair?

Liam: 26. Emma: 46. The chances are not the same.

Answer: No, Emma is more likely to win

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
“Less than 3” on a number cube is 1, 2 and 3.List the outcomes carefully: only 1 and 2.
3 red, 5 blue, so P(red) = 35.Compare with ALL the outcomes: 38.
3 colours, so each colour is 13.Look at the size of each part of the spinner.
“5 tails in a row, so heads is due.”A coin has no memory. Heads is still 12.

faq.q: What do Grade 5 students learn about probability in BC?
faq.a: The BC Grade 5 math curriculum lists probability experiments with single events or outcomes. Students list the outcomes, describe how likely an event is (impossible to certain), write the probability as a fraction, predict results and compare them with an experiment.

faq.q: What is the difference between an outcome and an event?
faq.a: An outcome is one possible result, such as rolling a 4. An event is a group of outcomes, such as rolling an even number (2, 4 or 6).

faq.q: How do you write a probability as a fraction?
faq.a: Put the number of outcomes you want over the total number of equally likely outcomes. A bag with 3 red and 5 blue marbles gives a probability of 3/8 for red, not 3/5.
A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning. Winning on heads or tails is fair (1/2 each), but winning on 1 or 2 against 3 to 6 on a number cube is not (2/6 and 4/6).

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. How many possible outcomes are there?
items.e: The cube can land on 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6: 6 outcomes. 21 adds the numbers (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) instead of counting them.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which is NOT a possible outcome?
items.e: The faces show 1 to 6, so 7 can never come up. 1 and 6 are the smallest and largest faces.

items.q: You take one marble from this bag without looking. What are the possible outcomes?
items.e: Every marble is red or blue, so the outcomes are red or blue. 3 and 2 are how many of each colour, not outcomes. There is no yellow marble.

items.q: R is red, B is blue and Y is yellow. How many different colours can this spinner land on?
items.e: The spinner has 6 sections, but only 3 colours: red, blue and yellow. 6 counts the sections, not the colours.

items.q: Cards numbered 5 to 12 are shuffled. You pick one. How many possible outcomes are there?
items.e: The cards are 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12: 8 cards. 12 − 5 = 7 forgets one card. 17 adds 5 + 12.

items.q: Which outcome is impossible on this spinner?
items.e: All the numbers (2, 4, 6, 8) are even, so an odd number can never come up. 6 and 8 are greater than 5, so that can happen.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which outcomes make the event “roll a number greater than 4”?
items.e: Greater than 4 means bigger than 4, so 4 itself does not count: 5 and 6. 1, 2, 3 and 4 are the outcomes that are NOT greater than 4.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which outcomes make the event “roll an even number”?
items.e: The even numbers on the cube are 2, 4 and 6. Don’t forget 6. There is no 0 on the cube. 1, 3 and 5 are odd.

items.q: Are the 4 outcomes on this spinner equally likely?
c: No, green is the most likely
Yes, because every spinner is fair
No, red is at the top
Yes, all 4 sections are the same size
items.e: Each colour has one section and all the sections are the same size, so yes: each colour is 14. Where a colour sits does not matter.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. Which outcome is more likely?
items.e: There are 5 green marbles and only 1 purple marble, so green is more likely. Two colours does not mean the two outcomes are equally likely.

items.q: Are the 3 outcomes on this spinner equally likely?
c: No, red covers more of the spinner
Yes, each colour has one section
items.e: Red covers 12 but blue and yellow cover only 14 each. Red is more likely. Count the size of the parts, not the number of colours.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 12 are shuffled. You pick one. How many outcomes make the event “a multiple of 3”?
items.e: The multiples of 3 are 3, 6, 9 and 12: 4 cards. 3 forgets the 12. 8 is the number of cards that are NOT multiples of 3.

items.q: The spinner has 8 equal sections. How many outcomes are less than 4?
items.e: Less than 4 means 1, 2 or 3: 3 outcomes. 4 wrongly counts the 4. 5 counts 4 to 8, the numbers that are NOT less than 4.

items.q: A bag has 2 red, 2 blue and 2 yellow marbles. You take one without looking. Which is true?
items.e: Each colour has 2 marbles out of 6, so all 3 colours are equally likely. The 2 is how many of each colour, not the number of outcomes.

items.q: A box has 12 muffins: 5 blueberry, 4 banana and 3 bran. Wei takes one without looking. Which kind is least likely?
items.e: There are fewer bran muffins (3) than banana (4) or blueberry (5), so bran is least likely. 3 kinds does not mean equally likely.

items.q: Ji-woo did a spinner experiment. How many trials (spins) did she do?
items.e: Each spin is one trial. Add the results: 8 + 7 + 5 = 20 spins. 3 is the number of outcomes (colours), not trials.

items.q: Lucas spins a spinner with red, blue and green sections 30 times and writes down each colour. What are the outcomes, and what is the number of trials?
items.e: An outcome is a result that can happen: red, blue or green. A trial is one spin, and he spins 30 times. So 3 outcomes, 30 trials.

items.q: The letters of VANCOUVER are written on cards, one letter on each card. You pick one card. Which is true?
items.e: VANCOUVER has 9 letters, so 9 cards. V is on 2 cards, so there are only 8 different letters: V, A, N, C, O, U, E, R.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 25 are shuffled. You pick one. How many outcomes have the digit 2 in them?
items.e: They are 2, 12, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25: 8 cards. 9 counts 22 twice, but it is only one card. 2 and 3 forget the numbers in the twenties.

items.q: Hana says rolling a number cube has 2 outcomes, “6” and “not 6”, so the probability of a 6 is 12. What is her mistake?
c: She should say 21
items.e: “Not 6” is 5 outcomes (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and “6” is only 1 outcome. They are not equally likely, so P(6) = 16, not 12.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which word describes rolling a 7?
items.e: No face shows 7, so it can never happen: impossible. Unlikely means it can happen, but probably won’t.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which word describes rolling a number from 1 to 6?
items.e: Every face shows a number from 1 to 6, so it happens every time: certain.

items.q: You toss a coin. Which word describes getting heads?
items.e: Heads and tails each have the same chance, so heads is equally likely to happen or not happen.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. Which word describes taking a blue marble?
items.e: 9 of the 10 marbles are blue, so blue is likely. It is not certain, because there is 1 red marble.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. Which word describes taking a red marble?
items.e: Only 1 of the 10 marbles is red. It can happen, but probably won’t: unlikely. Impossible would mean there is no red marble at all.

items.q: Which word describes landing on red?
items.e: Red covers 34 of the spinner, more than half: likely. It is not certain, because blue can still come up.

items.q: Which word describes landing on blue?
items.e: Blue covers exactly half of the spinner, so blue is equally likely to come up or not.

items.q: Which word means the same as a probability of 0?
items.e: A probability of 0 means the event can never happen: impossible. A probability of 1 means certain.

items.q: Which event is certain?
c: Getting a red marble from a bag of red and blue
Rolling a 6 on a number cube
items.e: The days of the week always come in the same order, so Monday after Sunday is certain. The others can happen, but not every time.

items.q: Which event is impossible?
c: Taking a red marble from a bag of red and blue marbles
Landing on blue on a red and blue spinner
Taking a green marble from a bag of red and blue marbles
Rolling a 1 on a number cube
items.e: There are no green marbles in the bag, so taking green can never happen. The others can happen.

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is close to 0 but not at 0: unlikely. Impossible would be exactly at 0.

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is between 12 and 1, close to 1: likely. Certain would be exactly at 1.

items.q: Which event is likely?
c: Snow falls in Victoria on Canada Day
Rolling a 2 on a number cube
Snow falls at Whistler sometime in January
items.e: Whistler is in the mountains and it almost always snows there in winter, so that is likely. Snow on July 1 in Victoria is close to impossible. A coin is equally likely. A 2 is unlikely (16).

items.q: Which fraction describes an unlikely event?
items.e: 110 is between 0 and 12, close to 0: unlikely. 910 is likely and 1010 = 1 is certain.

items.q: Which word describes a probability of 56?
items.e: 56 is more than 12 but less than 1: likely. It is not certain, because it is not 66.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. Order the colours from least likely to most likely.
items.e: Yellow has 1 marble, blue 3 and red 6. From least to most likely: yellow, blue, red.

items.q: On which spinner is landing on red unlikely?
items.e: On spinner C red is a small part (18), so red can happen but probably won’t. A is certain, B is equally likely and D is impossible.

items.q: On which spinner is landing on blue certain?
items.e: Spinner B is all blue, so it lands on blue every time. On A blue is only likely, because red can still come up.

items.q: Liam rolls a number cube 10 times and never gets a 6. He says rolling a 6 is impossible. What is wrong?
c: A 6 is on the cube, so it is unlikely, not impossible
A 6 is now certain on the next roll
items.e: One face shows 6, so a 6 can always happen. Its probability is 16: unlikely, not impossible. It is not “due” either.

items.q: Ava’s spinner is 78 green and 18 white. She says landing on green is certain. What is wrong?
c: It is likely, not certain: white can still come up
items.e: 78 is close to 1, but not 1. White covers 18, so green is likely, not certain.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a 3?
items.e: There are 6 equally likely outcomes and only one of them is 3: 16. 36 uses the 3 as the count, but only one face shows a 3. 61 is upside down.

items.q: The spinner has 5 equal sections. What is the probability of landing on 4?
items.e: 4 is on 1 of the 5 equal sections: 15. 14 compares the 4 with the other 4 sections, not with all 5.

items.q: A bag has 2 red and 3 blue marbles. You take one without looking. What is the probability of red?
items.e: There are 2 + 3 = 5 marbles and 2 are red: 25. 23 compares red with blue, not with all 5 marbles. Two colours does not mean 12.

items.q: The spinner has 6 equal sections: R is red and B is blue. What is the probability of red?
items.e: 2 of the 6 equal sections are red: 26. 24 compares red with blue. 46 is blue. 62 is upside down.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a number less than 3?
items.e: Less than 3 means 1 or 2: 2 of the 6 outcomes, so 26. 36 wrongly counts the 3. 46 is the chance of 3 or more.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of NOT rolling a 6?
items.e: Not a 6 means 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5: 5 of the 6 outcomes, so 56. 16 is the chance of rolling a 6.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on blue?
items.e: Blue covers one quarter of the spinner: 14. 13 counts the 3 colours, but red is bigger than blue.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. What is the probability of green?
items.e: There are 4 + 1 + 3 = 8 marbles and 4 are green: 48. 44 compares green with the other 4 marbles. 13 counts colours, not marbles.

items.q: Red is in two small parts. Each one is 18 of the spinner. What is the probability of red?
items.e: 18 + 18 = 28 (= 14). 25 counts 2 of the 5 sections, but the sections are not the same size.

items.q: A number cube has the numbers 1, 1, 2, 2, 2 and 3 on its faces. What is the probability of rolling a 2?
items.e: 3 of the 6 faces show a 2: 36. 13 counts the 3 different numbers, but 2 is on more faces than 1 or 3.

items.q: On which spinner is the probability of blue 14?
items.e: On spinner C blue has 2 of the 8 equal sections: 28 = 14. Spinner A has 4 sections, but blue covers half of it.

items.q: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 yellow marbles. What is the probability of NOT taking red?
items.e: Not red means blue or yellow: 5 + 2 = 7 of the 10 marbles, so 710. 510 forgets the yellow marbles. 310 is the chance of red.

items.q: The letters of KAMLOOPS are written on 8 cards. You pick one card without looking. What is the probability of O?
items.e: KAMLOOPS has 8 letters and 2 of them are O: 28. 27 counts the 7 different letters. 26 compares the O cards with the other 6 cards.

items.q: The letters of NANAIMO are written on 7 cards. You pick one card without looking. What is the probability of N?
items.e: NANAIMO has 7 letters and 2 of them are N: 27. 15 counts the 5 different letters (N, A, I, M, O). 25 compares the N cards with the other 5 cards.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 12 are shuffled. You pick one. What is the probability of a multiple of 4?
items.e: The multiples of 4 are 4, 8 and 12: 3 of the 12 cards, so 312. 412 uses the 4 from the question. 212 forgets the 12. 912 is the chance of NOT a multiple of 4.

items.q: A drawer has 12 socks: 5 black, 4 white and 3 grey. Owen takes one sock without looking. What is the probability that it is white or grey?
items.e: White or grey: 4 + 3 = 7 of the 12 socks, so 712. 75 compares with the 5 black socks and is greater than 1.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 4 blue marbles. Nadia says the probability of red is 34. What is her mistake?
c: She compared red with blue, not with all 7 marbles
It should be 12 because there are 2 colours
She should write 43
Nothing, 34 is right
items.e: A probability compares with ALL the outcomes. There are 3 + 4 = 7 marbles, so P(red) = 37. She compared red with blue instead of with all 7 marbles.

items.q: A bag has 10 marbles. The probability of red is 25. How many red marbles are there?
items.e: 25 = 410, so 4 of the 10 marbles are red. 2 uses the numerator without changing to tenths. 6 is the number that are not red.

items.q: Mateo wants a spinner with 8 equal sections where the probability of green is 34. How many sections should be green?
items.e: 34 = 68, so 6 of the 8 sections should be green. 3 uses the numerator without changing to eighths. 2 is the number that are not green.

items.q: A bag has 3 green marbles and some blue marbles. The probability of green is 14. How many blue marbles are there?
items.e: 14 = 312, so there are 12 marbles in total. 12 − 3 = 9 blue. 12 is the total, not the number of blue marbles.

sets.title: Predict, then compare with the results

items.q: Liam rolls a number cube 60 times. About how many times should he expect to roll a 6?
items.e: A 6 has a probability of 16. 16 of 60 is 60 ÷ 6 = 10, so about 10. About 6 uses the number on the face.

items.q: Olivia tosses a coin 100 times. How many heads should she predict?
items.e: Half of 100 is 50. Results change from one experiment to the next, so predict about 50, not exactly 50.

items.q: Chloe spins this spinner 40 times. About how many times should she expect red?
items.e: Red is 34 of the spinner. 40 ÷ 4 = 10, and 3 × 10 = 30, so about 30. About 10 is for blue. About 20 thinks 2 colours means 12.

items.q: Kai spins this spinner 80 times. About how many times should he expect green?
items.e: Green is 14 of the spinner. 80 ÷ 4 = about 20. About 40 thinks “green or not green” is 12. About 60 is for the other 3 colours.

items.q: A bag has 1 red and 4 blue marbles. Owen takes a marble, records the colour and puts it back. He does this 50 times. About how many times should he get red?
items.e: P(red) = 15. 50 ÷ 5 = 10, so about 10. About 12 uses 14 (red compared with blue). About 40 is for blue.

items.q: Noah tosses a coin 20 times and gets 9 heads. What fraction of his tosses were heads?
items.e: Heads came up 9 times in 20 tosses: 920. 12 is the prediction, not the result. 911 compares heads with tails.

items.q: Simran’s class recorded 20 spins. In what fraction of the spins did red come up?
items.e: Red came up 12 times in 20 spins: 1220. 128 compares red with blue and is greater than 1. 820 is blue.

items.q: In what fraction of Sofia’s spins did red come up?
items.e: Red came up 9 times in 30 spins: 930. 921 compares red with the other 21 spins. 13 would be the prediction for 3 equal colours.

items.q: Lucas spins a spinner with 3 equal sections (red, blue, yellow) 30 times. He predicts about 10 reds and gets 11. What does this show?
c: The result is close to the prediction
He will get exactly 10 next time
items.e: 30 ÷ 3 = 10, so about 10 reds is a good prediction. 11 is only 1 more: close to the prediction. Results are rarely exactly the same as the prediction.

items.q: Ji-woo spins a spinner that is half red 10 times. Red comes up only 3 times. What does this show?
c: Not much: a few spins can be far from the prediction
Red should come up exactly 5 times
The chance of red must be 310
items.e: She predicts about 5 reds in 10 spins, but with only 10 spins luck changes the results a lot. A few spins can be far from the prediction. She should do many more spins.

items.q: How do these results compare with the prediction?
c: 4 will come up more next time
The number cube must be unfair
Close: each number should come up about 10 times
items.e: Prediction: 16 of 60 = 10 for each number. The results are all between 8 and 12, which is close to the prediction. Small differences are normal.

items.q: Ava tosses a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. Ethan tosses a coin 200 times and gets 104 heads. Whose results are closer to the prediction (half heads)?
items.e: Ava got 710 heads, which is 210 more than 12. Ethan got 104200, only 4200 more than 12. So Ethan’s results are closer.

items.q: Why are Ethan’s results (200 tosses) closer to the prediction than Ava’s (10 tosses)?
c: Big experiments are always exactly right
More trials usually get closer to the prediction
Ethan tossed the coin more carefully
items.e: With only a few trials, luck changes the results a lot. More trials usually get closer to the prediction, but not exactly.

items.q: Before each soccer game, a coin is tossed to decide which team starts. Tails has come up 5 games in a row. What is the probability of heads at the next game?
items.e: The coin has no memory. Every toss is a new trial, so heads is still 12. Heads is not “due” after a lot of tails.

items.q: Harjot has rolled a number cube 12 times without getting a 6. What is the probability of a 6 on the next roll?
items.e: The number cube does not remember earlier rolls. A 6 is still 16. It is not certain (1), even after a long wait.

items.q: Three groups spin the same spinner 20 times each. Red comes up 9, 13 and 8 times. Use all the results: in what fraction of the spins did red come up?
items.e: Add the results: 9 + 13 + 8 = 30 reds in 20 + 20 + 20 = 60 spins: 3060. Using all 60 spins is better than one group. 3020 is greater than 1.

items.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, blue, yellow and green. At the school fun fair, red comes up 98 times in 200 spins. What do the results suggest?
c: Red will stop coming up soon
The spinner is probably not fair
200 spins are too few to tell
items.e: Prediction: 14 of 200 = 50 reds. 98 is almost double that, after many spins, so the spinner is probably not fair.

items.q: At hockey practice, Leah scores on 8 of her 20 shots. Next practice she takes 10 shots. About how many goals should she predict?
items.e: She scored on 820 = 410 of her shots. So in 10 shots, predict about 4 goals. 8 was for 20 shots, not 10.

items.q: Owen counts 40 cars passing his school in Surrey. 14 of them are white. About how many of the next 20 cars should be white?
items.e: 20 cars is half of 40, so predict about half of 14: about 7. About 6 comes from 20 − 14.

items.q: A bag has 20 marbles. Mei takes one, records its colour and puts it back. She does this 40 times and gets red 10 times. About how many red marbles are in the bag?
items.e: Red came up 1040 = 14 of the time. 14 of 20 is 5, so there are about 5 red marbles. 10 is how many times red came up, not how many are in the bag.

items.q: In a game, Emma wins if a coin lands on heads and Lucas wins if it lands on tails. Is the game fair?
c: No, Lucas is more likely to win
Yes, each has a probability of 12
No, Emma is more likely to win
items.e: A game is fair when every player has the same chance of winning. Heads and tails are each 12, so the game is fair.

items.q: Simran and Arjun roll a number cube. Simran wins on 1 or 2. Arjun wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6. Is the game fair?
c: No, Arjun is more likely to win
No, Simran is more likely to win
Yes, both of them have numbers
items.e: Simran: 26. Arjun: 46. The chances are not equal, so the game is not fair: Arjun is more likely to win.

items.q: On the BC Ferries trip to Nanaimo, Owen and Leah play with a number cube. Owen wins on a 6. Leah wins on a 1. On any other number they roll again. Is the game fair?
c: No, most rolls are a tie
Yes, a 6 and a 1 are each 16
No, Leah is more likely to win
items.e: Each number is on one face, so a 6 and a 1 both have a probability of 16. The game is fair. A bigger number is not more likely.

items.q: Kai wins if a number cube shows an even number. Which rule for Ethan makes the game fair?
c: Ethan wins on a number less than 6
Ethan wins on an odd number
Ethan wins on a 5 or a 6
items.e: Kai has 2, 4, 6: 36. Odd numbers (1, 3, 5) are also 36, so the game is fair. A 1 is only 16, and 5 or 6 is 26.

items.q: Jasleen and Harjot pick a card from cards numbered 1 to 10. Jasleen wins on 1 to 5. Harjot wins on 6 to 10. Is the game fair?
c: Yes, each has 5 of the 10 cards
No, Harjot has the bigger numbers
items.e: Jasleen has 5 cards (1 to 5) and Harjot has 5 cards (6 to 10): 510 each. The game is fair. How big the numbers are does not matter.

items.q: Chloe wins if the spinner lands on red. Ryan wins if it lands on blue or green. Is the game fair?
c: No, Chloe has the biggest section
Yes, each has a probability of 12
items.e: Chloe: 12. Ryan: 14 + 14 = 12. Both have 12, so the game is fair.

items.q: Mei wins on red. Mateo wins on blue. On yellow, nobody wins and they spin again. Is the game fair?
c: No, yellow is a third player
No, Mei is more likely to win
Yes, red and blue are each 13
items.e: Mei and Mateo each have one equal section: 13 each. Yellow does not help either player, so the game is fair.

items.q: Zara wins on red. Harjot wins on blue. Is the game fair?
c: No, Harjot is more likely to win: blue has 3 sections
No, Zara is more likely to win
items.e: Red covers 12 = 48. Blue has 3 small sections: 38. 48 > 38, so Zara is more likely to win. Look at the size of the parts, not the number of sections.

items.q: Wei and Nadia roll a number cube. Wei wins on a number less than 4. Nadia wins on a number greater than 4. Is the game fair?
c: Yes, they both have 4 in the rule
No, Nadia is more likely to win
No, Wei is more likely to win
items.e: Less than 4: 1, 2, 3 (36). Greater than 4: 5, 6 (26). Wei is more likely to win. 4 is not the middle of 1 to 6.

items.q: A bag has 4 red and 2 blue marbles. Nadia wins on red and Owen wins on blue. How many blue marbles must be added to make the game fair?
items.e: For a fair game there must be as many blue as red: 4 blue. 4 − 2 = 2 more blue marbles. 4 is how many blue there should be in total, not how many to add.

items.q: Ryan and Kai play with 10 cards. Ryan wins on a red card and Kai wins on a black card. 6 cards are red and 4 are black. How many red cards must be changed to black to make the game fair?
items.e: A fair game needs 5 red and 5 black. Change 1 red card: then there are 5 red and 5 black. 2 is the difference 6 − 4, but changing one card takes one from red AND adds one to black.

items.q: Sofia wins on red and Liam wins on blue. Which spinner makes the game fair?
items.e: On spinner B red and blue each cover 2 of 4 equal sections: 24 each. Spinner C also has 2 red and 2 blue sections, but they are not the same size: red is 58.

items.q: At the school fun fair, a spinner has 8 equal sections and 1 of them wins a prize. 40 students spin once each. About how many students should win a prize?
items.e: P(prize) = 18. 40 ÷ 8 = 5, so about 5 students. About 35 is the number who should NOT win.

items.q: Arjun needs to land on green to win. Spinner A has 4 equal sections and 1 is green. Spinner B has 8 equal sections and 3 are green. Which spinner should he choose?
c: Spinner A, its green section is bigger
items.e: Spinner A: 14 = 28. Spinner B: 38. 38 > 28, so Spinner B gives a better chance.

items.q: At the school fun fair, Box A has 10 tickets and 3 of them win. Box B has 5 tickets and 2 of them win. Which box gives a better chance of winning?
c: Box A, it has more winning tickets
items.e: Box A: 310. Box B: 25 = 410. 410 > 310, so Box B is better, even though Box A has more winning tickets.

items.q: Bag A has 3 red and 1 blue marble. Bag B has 5 red and 5 blue marbles. You win on red. Which bag should you choose?
c: Bag B, it has more red marbles
items.e: Bag A: 34. Bag B: 510 = 12. 34 is more than 12, so Bag A is better, even though Bag B has more red marbles.

items.q: Game A: you win if a spinner with 3 equal sections lands on red. Game B: you win if a number cube shows 5 or 6. Which game gives a better chance of winning?
c: Game B, it has 2 winning numbers
items.e: Game A: 13. Game B: 26 = 13. The chances are the same.

items.q: Ji-woo wins on heads and Nadia wins on tails. After 20 tosses, Ji-woo has won 13 times. Nadia says the game is not fair. Is she right?
c: No, Nadia will win the next 6 tosses
No, heads and tails are each 12; 20 tosses can vary
items.e: The coin gives each player 12, so the game is fair. With only 20 tosses, results like 13 and 7 can happen. The game is still fair. The coin does not “owe” Nadia any wins.

items.q: A bag has 3 red, 3 blue and 2 green marbles. Wei wins on red, Mei wins on blue and Kai wins on green. Which change makes the game fair?
items.e: For a fair game each colour needs the same number of marbles. With 1 more green, there are 3 red, 3 blue and 3 green: 39 each. Adding 2 green would give Kai 4 marbles.

items.q: For the Terry Fox Run, Ms. Gill’s class makes 12 job cards, and 3 of them say “hand out water”. Each student picks a card and puts it back. If 24 students pick, about how many should get “hand out water”?
items.e: P(hand out water) = 312 = 14. 14 of 24 is 24 ÷ 4 = about 6. About 3 is the number of cards. About 8 comes from 24 ÷ 3.
